title: Building an offer that justifies a higher rate for Mobile beauty
audience: Mobile beauty therapists who quote per treatment, per visit or per package, and want a price that covers travel, set-up, products and the client’s confidence in a treatment given at home.
learningOutcomes: Write a mobile beauty offer with a clear outcome, time frame, client inputs and risk
Show travel, set-up and product costs as visible lines rather than hidden extras
Price treatments and packages on value, and check each one against cost and time

instruction.heading: A bad offer versus a good offer
instruction.body: “I do facials” is a service. “A 60-minute facial at your home, with a skin check before we start, a clean-down of the treatment area and a written aftercare note to take away” is an offer. The client buys the treatment, the time it takes and the certainty that it will be done safely in their own space, without a salon visit.

instruction.heading: The five parts of a mobile offer
instruction.body: Name the outcome in plain words, and do not describe a result the treatment cannot deliver. Give the visit length, including set-up and clean-down. List what the client provides, such as a clear treatment space, a firm surface and a power point if you need one. Add one certainty element, such as a skin check before the treatment and a written aftercare note. Set the risk you carry, such as the fix-first step in the next point. Write the scope and exclusions down, because a written quote becomes binding once it is accepted (business.gov.au, Prepare quotes). The research found no Australian operator price list for mobile beauty, so set the price from your own cost and time.

instruction.heading: Reducing friction for the client
instruction.body: Make the booking, access and handover simple. Confirm the address, parking or entry and any stairs before the visit. A client who does not have to travel or organise a room is paying for convenience, and each step you remove from their side supports a higher price.

instruction.heading: Guarantees, fix-first and consumer law
instruction.body: A guarantee must be something you can deliver and afford. For services, a business must be given a reasonable chance to fix a minor fault free of charge (Consumer Victoria, last updated 13 October 2023). That source does not set a length for the fix window, so choose one you can keep. A written warranty is an optional extra that sits on top of the consumer guarantees, and a “no refunds” line does not override a customer’s rights for services (business.gov.au, Warranties and refunds). The research found no source on skin-result claims, so do not publish any until you have evidence you can show.

instruction.heading: Treatment tiers, the total and packages
instruction.body: Stepped options work when each higher level adds something the client can see, such as a longer treatment or an added step. Jobber’s good-better-best examples, published May 2021 and updated 8 October 2024, use this pattern for trade services, but none of its examples is a beauty service. Show one clear total for the visit, with the travel charge on its own line, and say whether GST is included (ACCC, Setting prices: what’s allowed). A prepaid package is a prepaid service, so check the consumer rules before you sell one. Under the personal services guide, a business must not take payment for a service it cannot supply in a reasonable time. The research did not state a package discount, so do not quote one without checking it.

procedure: Write the outcome for one treatment, such as a facial at home, in one sentence a client would repeat.
Set the visit length, including set-up, clean-down and travel, and record how often you finish inside it.
List what the client must provide, and cut each step you can.
Add one certainty element, such as a skin check before the treatment and a written aftercare note.
Decide the fix-first window and any warranty, and check that you can afford both.
Price the treatment tiers and any package from value, then check the total against your cost and time.

workedExamples.situation: A mobile beauty therapist offers a 60-minute facial at a client’s home. The client asks whether the price includes travel, and whether the treatment is the same as the one in a salon.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Rewrite the offer so the client can compare it with a salon visit, and show the travel charge on the quote.
workedExamples.reasoning: The offer names the treatment, its length, the skin check, the clean-down and the aftercare note. The travel charge sits on its own line, with one total and a GST statement. The therapist does not claim that the home treatment equals a salon result, because no source supports that comparison. The price comes from the cost and time in the BP-05 and HBM-12 lessons, and this lesson gives no figure.

commonErrors.error: Promising a skin result that you cannot show
commonErrors.prevention: Describe the treatment and the steps you take. Do not state an outcome without evidence you can show.

commonErrors.error: Selling a package with no written terms, expiry or cancellation rule
commonErrors.prevention: Write the terms and check the prepaid-service and gift-card rules for your state before you sell it.

commonErrors.error: Adding a travel fee after the client has agreed to the price
commonErrors.prevention: Show the travel charge as its own line on the written quote before the visit.
State your fix-first policy and the client’s statutory rights in plain words, and keep both consistent.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Registration and licence rules for beauty work are set by each state and territory. Victoria: councils register beauty therapy premises under the Public Health and Wellbeing Act 2008. The council listing read did not say how mobile operators are treated, so ask your council. Northern Territory: a business paid for beauty therapy must register. Queensland: beauty therapy needs no licence, but the infection control guidelines apply, and higher-risk services need a licence. New South Wales: a mobile operator working from a vehicle must notify the council for skin-penetration work, and it is not clear whether non-penetrating treatments need notification. Other states and territories were not verified. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Gap: no mobile-specific registration rule was confirmed in any state, and the research did not check the rules for South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania or the Australian Capital Territory for beauty work.

Consumer rules on prepaid services: a business must not take payment for a service it cannot supply in a reasonable time (Personal services guide, 2013, p. 10). Gift card rules apply to most cards and vouchers sold on or after 1 November 2019, with a minimum three-year expiry, and the sources read do not say whether memberships are covered. Check the rules for your state before you sell a package.
Business guidance only. This lesson gives no tax advice. Check the tax treatment of your income with a registered tax agent.

qualityStandard: Every offer states the outcome, the visit length, the client inputs, the certainty element and the risk, in writing before the visit.
The travel charge and GST status appear on the quote as separate, checkable lines.
No skin-result claim is published without evidence the business can show.
documentationEvidence: Written offer or treatment sheet, with the date it was issued
Visit-length record, compared with the stated visit length
Package terms, and the record of any fix-first or warranty request and its outcome
summary: A good offer promises a named treatment, a time frame, client inputs, certainty and a fair guarantee.
Show the travel charge and GST as visible lines, so the higher price is easy to see.
Charge for value you can show, and check the price against your cost and time.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which part of a mobile offer does the customer buy?
What should a guarantee be?
options: Impossible to claim on in any case
Only for new customers and friends
Something you can deliver and afford

officialReferences.covers: States that misleading statements about prices are prohibited. Publisher: ACCC.

Jobber Academy, 'Good, Better, Best Pricing Examples', https://getjobber.com/academy/good-better-best-pricing-examples/, published May 2021, updated 8 October 2024. Supports: stepped packages. Older than 2022; examples are not beauty services.

Personal services: an industry guide to the Australian Consumer Law (Consumer Victoria and ACCC), 2013, https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/library/publications/businesses/fair-trading/personal-services-an-industry-guide-to-the-australian-consumer-law.pdf. Supports: no payment taken for a service that cannot be supplied in a reasonable time (p. 10). Dated 2013.

Gaps: no dated Australian mobile beauty price list, travel fee or package evidence; no source on skin-result claims; Support at Home and NDIS do not name beauty in the parts checked; memberships are not stated in the federal or NSW gift card sources.
